- If sentiment shows strong bullish (e.g., +1.00) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment shows strong bearish (e.g., -1.00) in recent days, model tends to underestimate prices; increase downward bias or add early correction.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 5–10% in next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (e.g., 0.00 or 0.25), model often drifts toward mean reversion; align forecast with recent 5–7 day average if no strong sentiment signal.
- If true outcome shows strong divergence from forecast in first 5–7 days (e.g., >5% error), model may be overconfident; apply “early correction” rule: adjust forecast downward if sentiment is negative or volatility is high.
- Model tends to overpredict in early forecast horizon (e.g., 1–3 days) when sentiment is positive; apply “lag correction”: reduce forecast by 1–2% per day for first 3 days if sentiment is bullish.
- If sentiment history includes multiple +1.00 or -1.00 entries, model may be “sensitive to sentiment” and overreact; apply “sentiment dampening” rule: reduce forecast amplitude by 10–20% if sentiment is extreme.
